encounters.text: Why Do Your Toes Go Numb in the Snow? When your feet get cold, your body has a clever plan. It wants to keep your heart and brain warm first. So it squeezes the tiny blood tubes in your toes. Less warm blood flows down to your feet. Without that warm blood, your toes cool down even more. Soon the nerves in your toes slow down. They stop sending messages to your brain. That is why your toes feel numb, like they belong to someone else. When you warm up again, the blood rushes back. The nerves wake up all at once, which is why your toes tingle and itch.

encounters.text: Leafy Seadragons. Leafy seadragons are fish that live in cool, shallow water off southern Australia. They are related to seahorses. A leafy seadragon grows to about 35 centimetres long. Its body is covered in flaps that look like seaweed leaves. These flaps help it hide among the kelp. Its tiny fins are almost see-through, so it seems to drift like a loose piece of seaweed. Leafy seadragons are yellow, brown or green. They have no teeth. Instead, they suck up tiny shrimp through their long, thin snouts. Male seadragons carry the eggs on their tails until they hatch. Leafy seadragons are protected by law, so nobody is allowed to catch them.

encounters.frame: The Architect keeps a shelf of nature books in the Tower One hut. The Whyrella has opened one.
encounters.text: How Snow Gums Survive a Bushfire. Snow gums grow high in the mountains, where summer bushfires can sweep through the trees. A strong fire can kill every leaf and branch on a snow gum, but the tree is not finished. Hidden at the base of its trunk is a woody lump called a lignotuber. This lump stores food, and it is covered in sleeping buds. Because the lump is partly underground, the soil protects it from the heat of the flames. After the fire has passed, the burnt tree can no longer make food in its leaves. This change wakes the sleeping buds. They use the food stored in the lump to send up new green shoots. Within a few years, the shoots grow into a ring of new stems around the old, dead trunk. That is why many snow gums have several thin trunks instead of one thick one.

encounters.text: How a Guitar Makes Its Sound. When you pluck a guitar string, it moves backwards and forwards very quickly. This is called vibrating. A thick string vibrates more slowly than a thin one, so it makes a lower note. The vibrating string pushes on the air around it and makes tiny waves. On its own, a string is quite quiet, because it is too thin to move much air. That is why a guitar has a hollow wooden body. The string passes its shaking through the bridge into the thin wooden top of the guitar. The whole top starts to vibrate, and because it is much bigger than the string, it pushes far more air. The air inside the body bounces around and comes out of the round sound hole. By the time the sound reaches your ears, it is many times louder than the string alone. That is why you can hear a guitar from the back of a hall, even though its strings are thinner than spaghetti.

encounters.frame: Tully is reading up before the Architect's space camp. The Whyrella is reading over her shoulder.
encounters.text: Why Astronauts' Bones Get Weaker in Space. On Earth, your skeleton works hard every second of the day, even when you are just standing in line at the canteen. Gravity pulls your body towards the ground, so your bones must hold up your weight with every step. This constant load sends a signal to special cells inside your bones, telling them to keep building fresh, strong bone. On a space station, however, astronauts float, so their legs, hips and spine have almost no weight to carry. Without that load, the bone-building cells receive no signal and slow down, while other cells keep breaking old bone down at the usual rate. As a result, an astronaut can lose around one per cent of the bone in their hips and legs every month. The lost minerals travel into the blood, which is also why some astronauts develop painful kidney stones. Exercise machines that make astronauts push against heavy springs can slow this loss, because they create some of the load that gravity normally provides. Astronauts also eat foods rich in calcium and vitamin D, which their bodies need to build new bone. Even so, after returning to Earth, it can take years for their bones to fully recover.

encounters.success: It explains. It links causes and effects: no weight, no signal, less bone built, weaker bones.

parts: How an Avalanche Starts. Every snowfall leaves a new layer on the mountainside, so by late winter the snow is built up like the pages of an enormous book.

parts.tap: Some layers are packed hard by the wind, while others are made of loose, sugary crystals that barely stick to anything.
parts.reason: This explains why some layers are weak, which is where the trouble begins.

parts.tap: When heavy fresh snow piles on top of a weak layer, the weak layer is squeezed until it can barely hold the weight above it.
parts.reason: This explains what puts strain on the weak layer.

parts: The weak layer is now like a shelf of thin glass holding up a pile of bricks. Then a trigger, such as a sudden warm day, a falling chunk of ice or even a single skier, can make it collapse.

parts.tap: Because the slope is steep, the whole slab of snow above the broken layer begins to slide.
parts.reason: This explains what happens once the layer breaks, and why.

parts.tap: Before you leave the hut, always check the avalanche warning board and never ski alone.
As the slab speeds up, it breaks into blocks and churns up more snow, until it races downhill faster than a car.
parts.reason: This explains how the avalanche grows as it falls.

parts: That is why a small crack near the top of a slope can become a huge, roaring wall of snow by the bottom. Most avalanches happen on slopes that are about as steep as a playground slide, because steeper slopes shed their snow before it can build up.

encounters.text: How a Compass Finds North. Deep inside the Earth, a core of hot, liquid iron is constantly churning, and this movement turns the whole planet into a gigantic, weak magnet. Like any magnet, the Earth has two magnetic poles, one near the North Pole and one near the South Pole, and invisible lines of magnetic force loop between them. Scientists call the space around a magnet, where its pull can be felt, a magnetic field. A compass needle is a thin sliver of magnetised metal, balanced on a pin so that it can spin with almost no friction. Because the needle is a tiny magnet itself, its ends are pulled by the Earth's magnetic field, and the needle swings until it lines up with those invisible lines. The end marked in red is attracted towards the magnetic pole in the north, which is why it always settles pointing that way. However, the magnetic pole is not in exactly the same place as the North Pole on a map, and it slowly wanders over the years. Near the far north of Canada, the gap between the two can be so large that a compass is almost useless. That is why a compass and a map can disagree by a few degrees.

encounters.success: It explains. It links causes: a churning core makes a magnet, which pulls the needle round to point north.

encounters.text: Tower Four Gets a Makeover. Last Thursday, after three months of planning, Room 6 finally painted a mural on the bare concrete wall at the foot of Tower Four. The day began badly: at eight o'clock the wall was still coated in frost, so Ms Petrakis sent everyone back inside for hot chocolate while the sun did its work. By ten, the wall was dry enough for the first coat of sky blue, which went on with rollers tied to broom handles. After recess, small groups took turns on the scaffolding to paint the snow gums, the ladders and, at Indi's insistence, a crimson rosella the size of a car. Just before lunch, a gust of wind knocked over a tin of red paint, and for a few panicked minutes it looked as if the rosella had sprung a leak. Zed rescued the moment by turning the spill into a row of fallen leaves. In the afternoon, the class added the outlines and signed their names in the bottom corner. Parents arrived at three for the unveiling, and the principal declared it the brightest thing on the island. Room 6 would like to thank the hardware store for donating the paint.
